en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Nissaggiya Section (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Pairs 3.
The Training Rule on the Exchange of Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having exchanged a robe with a certain bhikkhunī, made use of it.
Then that bhikkhunī, having folded that robe, laid it aside.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā said this to that bhikkhunī:
“Venerable lady, where is that robe which was exchanged by me with you?
Then that bhikkhunī brought out the robe and showed it to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā said this to that bhikkhunī:
“Come now, sister, this robe is yours; bring back this robe! What is yours is yours alone, and what is mine is mine alone. Bring it back; give back what is your own! Thus she tore it away.
Then that bhikkhunī informed the bhikkhunīs of this matter.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:

“How indeed could the noble lady Thullanandā, having exchanged a robe with a bhikkhunī, then take it back? Then those bhikkhunīs informed the bhikkhus of this matter. The bhikkhus informed the Blessed One of this matter … [as before] … The Blessed One then addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back, she commits an offense of wrong-doing. [The Blessed One then laid down the rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back, she commits an offense of wrong-doing. [The Blessed One then laid down the exception: “I allow you, bhikkhunīs, to take back a robe that was exchanged under these five conditions: if it was exchanged by mistake, if it was exchanged through delusion, if it was exchanged through intoxication, if it was exchanged while insane, or if it was exchanged while possessed by a malevolent spirit. These are the five conditions. [The Blessed One then laid down the full rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back—unless it was exchanged under one of these five conditions—she commits an offense of wrong-doing. [The Blessed One then laid down the penalty: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back—unless it was exchanged under one of these five conditions—she commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya). [The Blessed One then laid down the definition: “In this case, ‘exchanged’ means: ‘I will give you this robe; you must give me that robe. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already made use of it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already washed it, dyed it, or finished using it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it away, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already destroyed it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already lost it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already discarded it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it as a gift, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already sold it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already bartered it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already worn it out, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a third party, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already returned it to her, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already disposed of it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already abandoned it, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it away as a gift to a layperson, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a novice monk or novice nun, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a female probationer or a female trainee, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male probationer or a male trainee, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male lay follower or a female lay follower, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a king or a royal official, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a thief or a robber, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a fire-worshipper or a naked ascetic, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a wanderer or a female wanderer, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male or female householder, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male or female slave, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male or female servant, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male or female guest, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male or female visitor, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has already given it to a male or female relative, she commits an offense entailing confession. [The Blessed One then laid down the further rule: “If a bhikkhunī, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, should take it back after the other has
“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā, having exchanged a robe with another nun, then took it back?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her... [as before]...
"How indeed, monks, could the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having exchanged a robe with another bhikkhunī, take it back?
This, monks, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule: [The rule follows]"
“Whatever nun, having exchanged a robe with another nun, should later say:
‘Come, sister, bring back your robe; here is your robe. What was yours is yours alone, and what was mine is mine alone.
Bring this back; take back what is your own,’ and should either take it back herself or cause it to be taken back, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.”
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
... pe ... this is the nun intended in this context.
"Together with a nun" means together with another nun.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes that is suitable for assignment and is of the lowest quality.
"Having exchanged" means...
Whether [taking] much from little, or little from much.
"Should take away" means she herself takes it away; there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya pācittiya).
"Causes to be confiscated":
if she commands another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Once commanded, even if she confiscates much, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It should be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to a single bhikkhunī.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
…pe…
“Venerable ladies, this robe-cloth of mine, which was taken back after being exchanged with a bhikkhunī, is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
…pe… “May [the individual] give it back” …pe… “May they give it back” …pe…
“I give it to the noble lady.

If she perceives one who is fully ordained as being fully ordained, and having exchanged a robe, she either takes it back herself or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If she is doubtful regarding one who is fully ordained, and having exchanged a robe, she either takes it back herself or causes it to be taken back, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If she has exchanged a robe with one who is fully ordained, perceiving her as not fully ordained, and then seizes it back or causes it to be seized, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If she exchanges another requisite and then seizes it back or causes it to be seized, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If she exchanges a robe or another requisite with one who is not fully ordained and then seizes it back or causes it to be seized, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is doubtful regarding one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as being not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if she gives it herself,
or if one takes it from her while she is entrusting it to her.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of one who is a first-offender.
The third training rule is concluded.
